AMEI: Dividend-paying companies chosen under Islamic investing principles, spread across technology, industrials and health care. The faith-based rules exclude banks and interest-heavy businesses, so it aims for equity income and steady payouts in a way that follows Sharia guidelines.
AMEM: Companies in developing countries, picked under Islamic investing principles, with technology close to half the fund and materials and health care behind. The faith-based screen leaves out banks and other interest-based businesses, giving emerging-market growth exposure that follows Sharia rules.
ARMH: A single-stock fund holding the US-listed shares of Arm, the British company whose chip designs sit inside nearly every smartphone. A built-in currency hedge softens moves between the pound and the dollar, so the fund follows Arm itself more purely.
ASMH: A single-stock fund holding the US-listed shares of ASML, the Dutch company that makes the machines used to print advanced computer chips. A built-in currency hedge dampens euro and dollar swings, leaving the fund riding on one vital company in the chip supply chain.
BEEZ: US companies of all sizes, led by industrials at about a third, with technology, health care and banks behind them. Managers pick the stocks actively, so it works as a broad core holding whose results rest on their choices rather than an index.
BSGR: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2027, so the fund acts like one government bond with a set end date. It suits savers targeting a goal around then, paying government-backed interest with none of the credit risk of company bonds.
BUYZ: Companies changing how people shop, pay and order: online retail and consumer brands are the biggest part, with technology and media firms behind. It is a growth bet on the shift to digital commerce around the world, favoring disruptors over traditional stores.
CBTY: Bitcoin with a partial safety net: over each roughly one-year period starting in July, it aims to absorb losses beyond the first 20 percent while capping gains. It trades away crash protection on smaller dips for more room to rise than tighter shielded versions.
CDPI: Dividend-paying stocks across banks, health care, technology and everyday consumer brands, paired with an options strategy meant to add extra income on top of the dividends. It is built for high payouts now, accepting that option selling gives up some stock gains.
DESK: Office and commercial property companies: the trusts that own office towers, business parks and other workplaces in the US. It pays property income, but it is a narrow bet on offices at a time when remote work keeps demand for desk space uncertain.
EFRA: Companies that build and run environmental infrastructure, mostly industrial firms with utilities behind them: water systems, waste handling and cleaner transport gear. It is a bet on the less glamorous side of going green, where spending comes from cities and long-term projects.
EPAI: Companies where artificial intelligence could change the business in a big way, led by technology at about 60 percent with industrials close behind. Managers hunt for firms at the turning point of adopting AI, so it is a growth bet wider than pure tech.
EPSV: Small and mid-sized US companies that look undervalued, led by industrials at a bit over a quarter, with banks and technology behind them. It is a value bet on the market's smaller names, so it can trail while big growth stocks lead.
FTIF: Companies picked because their businesses tend to hold up when inflation bites: energy producers are nearly half the fund, with industrial, materials and property firms behind. It is a defensive corner of the stock market meant to shine when prices elsewhere are rising fast.
GBHI: Riskier corporate bonds, the high yield kind often called junk bonds, picked one by one by Gabelli's managers for interest income. It aims for high payouts from below-investment-grade borrowers, which means more chance of defaults and bigger price swings than safer bond funds.
HBIL: US Treasury bills, the shortest government IOUs, maturing in a few weeks or months. It works like a parking spot for cash that pays a little interest, with almost no price movement and the full backing of the US government.
HSMV: Small and mid-sized US companies chosen for steadier share prices, leaning toward property, banking and utility stocks that usually move less. It aims to keep the growth potential of smaller companies while smoothing the ride, accepting that it will trail in strong rallies.
IBGK: US Treasury bonds scheduled to mature in 2054, bundled in a fund with a set end date decades away. The long wait means steady government interest, but prices that jump around a lot whenever interest rates change.
IBGL: US Treasury bonds that mature in December 2055, held in a fund with a built-in end date three decades away. Such long bonds pay steady government interest but their prices swing hard when interest rates move, far more than shorter bonds.
INDH: Indian companies across banks, consumer brands, energy and technology, with a currency hedge that cancels out swings between the rupee and the dollar. The hedge means returns follow the stocks themselves, which can help or hurt versus unhedged India funds depending on the rupee.
INDZ: Indian companies chosen by VanEck's managers, led by banks at about a third, with industrials, health care and materials behind. Unlike index funds for India, the hand-picked approach can lean into or away from sectors, so results depend on the managers' calls.
IPAV: Companies that build infrastructure outside the US: construction, engineering and materials firms split about evenly between industrials and materials. It is a bet on roads, ports and power projects across developed and emerging markets, moving with government building programs.
KAIT: Asian technology companies built around artificial intelligence: chip makers, software firms and data companies across the region make up nearly the whole fund. It is a focused bet on Asia's AI industry, so it adds currency and regional political swings to tech's usual ups and downs.
LITL: Small US companies, mostly health care, technology and banks, combined with an options overlay designed to add regular income. The mix aims for small-company growth plus payouts, a pairing most small-cap funds do not offer.
LTAX: Long-term municipal bonds from US states and cities, paying interest that is exempt from federal income tax. The long maturities mean higher tax-free payouts but prices that move a lot when interest rates change, so it suits investors in high tax brackets.
NUGY: An income strategy using derivatives on a leveraged gold miners fund, harvesting the miners' big price swings as regular payouts. It is a high-risk trade rather than a way to own gold: leverage resets and option caps can turn a miners' slump into steep losses.
PJIN: Companies from around the world, picked by PGIM's Jennison team as a core international holding. Managers choose stocks across developed markets rather than copying an index, so the mix shifts with where they find the strongest businesses.
PJSM: Small and medium-sized US companies picked by PGIM's Jennison team across all industries, aiming for a mix of steady growers and undervalued names. It is an actively managed core holding for the smaller end of the market, so it swings more than large-company funds.
PMJA: Large US stocks matching the broad S&P 500 mix, wrapped in options that cushion the opening slice of any fall over the year starting in January. The cushion costs some upside, since gains are capped, making it a gentler way to hold stocks.
PMMR: The broad US stock market through S&P 500 companies, combined with an options cushion that absorbs the first slice of losses over the year starting in March. Gains are capped in exchange, so it suits investors who want stocks with some protection underneath.
PMMY: Large US stocks, the same broad mix as the S&P 500, paired with options that cushion the first chunk of a fall over the one-year period starting in May. Gains are limited in exchange, making it a cautious route into the stock market.
PRIZ: Preferred shares, a hybrid between stocks and bonds that pays set dividends, mostly issued by banks and other big companies. It is built for steady income that usually pays more than regular bonds, though preferred prices still dip when markets fall.
PSWD: Cybersecurity companies screened for strong business quality, with technology names making up about 90 percent of the fund. It is a focused bet on spending to stop hackers and data breaches, a corner of tech that grows even when other budgets tighten.
PWRZ: Companies that own and run renewable power plants, mostly utilities generating wind and solar electricity around the world. It is built for income from selling clean power, so it behaves more like a steady utility than a high-growth green tech bet.
RBLY: An options strategy wrapped around Roblox stock, the gaming platform company, built to turn its price swings into regular income. It never simply holds the shares for growth, and if Roblox drops hard the fund can fall nearly as much while its gains stay capped.
REFA: Companies from developed countries outside the US, spread across drug makers, chip equipment, mining, banks and machinery firms. Columbia's research models tilt the mix toward their highest-rated names, aiming for a core international holding that does a bit better than plain index funds.
REMC: Mid-sized US companies, led by technology at about a fifth, with industrials, health care and banks behind them. Columbia's research models tilt toward their favorite names, aiming for a mid-cap core holding that edges past a plain index.
RESM: Small US companies across health care, technology, banks and industrials, chosen with Columbia's research models tilting toward the names scored best. It aims to beat a plain small-cap index by quiet stock picking rather than big sector bets.
RNTY: US real estate companies, mostly property-owning trusts, paired with an options program built to pay income at a target rate of 12 percent a year. It aims for rent-like payouts with extra option income, though property stocks still swing with the housing and rate cycle.
TFJL: Options on a fund of long-term US Treasury bonds, built with a floor meant to stop losses past a set point over the year starting each July. It is a defensive way to hold interest-rate bets: cushioned against deep bond sell-offs, capped if bonds rally hard.
THNR: Companies worldwide that stand to gain from weight loss drugs and treatments: drug makers, drug distributors and related health care firms make up the whole fund. It is a focused bet on one booming corner of medicine, so it swings with drug news and competition.
TINS: Stocks from countries outside the US, picked by Templeton's managers using on-the-ground research into each company's prospects. It is an actively run international holding, so its country and industry mix shifts with where the managers see the best value.
TIPC: Inflation-linked government bonds arranged in a ladder aimed at 2045, meaning their values and payouts rise with inflation. It is designed for savers planning spending around that year, paying out distributions along the way rather than holding everything to one end date.
TQQY: An income strategy built on options over a triple-leveraged Nasdaq fund, turning that fund's huge daily swings into regular payouts. It is among the riskiest income designs: leverage resets daily and the options cap gains, so losses in a tech slide can be severe.
UXJL: Options built to amplify the US stock market's gains over a one-year period starting in July, with no fixed cap on the boosted upside. The amplification cuts both ways, so falls are not softly cushioned, making it an aggressive, short-horizon bet rather than a core holding.
VCLN: Clean energy companies split fairly evenly between industrial manufacturers and utilities, with technology firms making up most of the rest. It covers the whole green power chain, from equipment makers to the utilities selling solar and wind electricity, and swings with energy policy.
WDGF: Defense companies from around the world: weapons makers, military aircraft and ship builders, and the tech firms that support them, with industrials about 90 percent of the fund. It is a global bet on military budgets, moving with government spending and world tensions.
YRAM: Memory and storage chip companies, the firms making the parts that hold data in computers and AI servers, plus options sold on them for income. It pairs a hot, cyclical corner of tech with monthly payouts, though the option sales limit gains in big rallies.
YSAG: Physical silver, held as bullion rather than through mining stocks or futures. Its price follows the metal itself, so it is a direct bet on silver, which tends to swing harder than gold and plays both precious metal and industrial roles.
ZTAX: Municipal bonds issued by states, cities and public projects across the US, paying interest that is designed to be free of federal and state income tax. It is built for investors in higher tax brackets who want steady, tax-free income.
